terms.definition: The whole sequence of events your body's security system runs through to detect, fight off, and remember a germ.
terms.function: Protects the body from pathogens by detecting them, destroying them, and keeping a record so future encounters are handled faster.
terms.whereItIs: Runs throughout the bloodstream and tissues, coordinated by white blood cells traveling wherever they're needed.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the reason you fight off most infections without ever feeling seriously sick, and the reason vaccines and lifelong immunity work at all.

terms.definition: The very first moment a germ crosses into the body and gets noticed by sensor cells stationed in the tissue.
terms.function: Sensor cells recognize the antigen markers on the pathogen's surface as foreign and release chemical alarm signals that call the rest of the immune system into action.
terms.whereItIs: Stage 1 of the diorama, at the tissue-barrier ridge on the far-left plinth, where the pathogen figure meets the sensor cell.
terms.whyItMatters: Nothing else in the immune response can happen until a pathogen is actually detected — a faster, more accurate detection means a faster, milder illness.

terms.definition: The stage where white blood cells travel toward the alarm signal — some eating germs directly, others directing the rest of the response.
terms.function: White blood cells (leukocytes) either engulf and digest the pathogen themselves or coordinate other immune cells, acting as the body's fast-arriving first soldiers.
terms.whereItIs: Stage 2 of the diorama, on the connecting groove between the detection and antibody-production plinths, where several white-blood-cell figures converge.
terms.whyItMatters: This general-purpose response can start acting within minutes, buying the body time while the slower, more precise antibody response is being built.

terms.definition: The stage where special white blood cells called plasma cells learn a pathogen's exact shape and mass-produce antibodies to match it.
terms.function: Plasma cells manufacture Y-shaped proteins called antibodies that bind tightly to one specific antigen, tagging that pathogen so it can be found and destroyed.
terms.whereItIs: Stage 3 of the diorama, at the center plinth, where small antibody proteins float just above the plasma-cell figure.
terms.whyItMatters: Antibodies are what make the immune response so precise — instead of attacking anything and everything, the body builds a custom-shaped weapon for this exact pathogen.

terms.definition: The stage where antibody-tagged pathogens are recognized and broken apart by phagocyte cells, clearing the infection.
terms.function: Phagocyte cells recognize the antibody tags and engulf the marked pathogen, breaking it into pieces and removing it from the body.
terms.whereItIs: Stage 4 of the diorama, right-of-center, where the fragmented pathogen pieces are shown being absorbed by a larger phagocyte figure.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the moment the infection is actually cleared — everything before it (detection, response, antibody production) exists to make this destruction possible.

terms.definition: The stage where a few of the cells that fought this pathogen become memory cells and stay in the body long-term.
terms.function: Memory cells keep a lasting record of the pathogen's shape, letting the body recognize and respond to it much faster if it ever returns — often before symptoms even start.
terms.whereItIs: Stage 5 of the diorama, at the far-right plinth, where the resting memory-cell figure sits inside a faint standby halo.
terms.whyItMatters: Immune memory is why you usually don't get sick from the same germ twice, and it's the exact mechanism vaccines use to protect you.

terms.definition: The body's fast, general-purpose defense — things like skin, mucus, and general white blood cells that fight any germ the same way, not just one specific kind.
terms.function: Acts within minutes to hours, providing an immediate barrier and first response before the body has time to build a pathogen-specific weapon.
terms.whereItIs: Present everywhere from birth — the skin, mucous membranes, and general-purpose white blood cells like macrophages, active at stage 2 (White blood cells respond).
terms.whyItMatters: Without this fast-acting first layer, even minor infections would have days to spread before any targeted defense arrived.

terms.definition: The body's slower-to-start but highly targeted defense that learns one pathogen's exact shape and builds custom antibodies to match it.
terms.function: Takes days to fully activate the first time, but produces antibodies and memory cells precisely matched to one pathogen, giving much stronger and longer-lasting protection.
terms.whereItIs: Driven by B cells and T cells, active at stages 3 through 5 (antibody production, pathogen destruction, and memory formation).
terms.whyItMatters: Adaptive immunity is what makes the body's second encounter with a germ so much faster and milder than the first — and it's the whole reason vaccines work.

terms.definition: A germ — such as a virus, bacterium, or fungus — that can cause disease.
terms.function: Invades the body and, left unchecked, damages cells or disrupts normal function, which is what the immune response exists to prevent.
terms.whereItIs: Can enter through the skin, airways, or digestive tract; shown crossing the tissue barrier at stage 1 of the diorama.
terms.whyItMatters: Every stage of the immune response exists because pathogens are constantly trying to get past the body's defenses.

terms.definition: A blood cell whose job is to find and destroy pathogens — the immune system's soldiers.
terms.function: Includes several types with different jobs: some engulf pathogens directly, others produce antibodies, and others kill infected cells.
terms.whereItIs: Circulates through blood and tissue, shown converging toward the alarm signal at stage 2 of the diorama.
terms.whyItMatters: White blood cells are the active, moving part of the immune system — without them, detecting a pathogen wouldn't be enough to actually stop it.

terms.definition: A unique marker on the surface of a pathogen that the immune system uses to recognize it as foreign.
terms.function: Acts like a fingerprint — sensor cells detect it at stage 1, and antibodies are custom-built at stage 3 to bind to it specifically.
terms.whereItIs: On the outer surface of the pathogen itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a distinct antigen to recognize, the immune system couldn't tell a harmful pathogen apart from the body's own healthy cells.

terms.definition: A Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells that binds tightly to one specific antigen, marking the pathogen for destruction.
terms.function: Locks onto a pathogen's antigen like a key fitting one specific lock, tagging it so phagocyte cells can find and destroy it.
terms.whereItIs: Produced by plasma cells at stage 3 of the diorama, then circulates to find and tag matching pathogens.
terms.whyItMatters: Antibodies are what make the adaptive immune response so precise — a targeted weapon built for one exact invader.

terms.definition: A type of white blood cell that turns into a plasma cell and produces antibodies.
terms.function: Once activated by recognizing a matching antigen, a B cell multiplies and becomes a plasma cell factory, churning out antibodies for that pathogen.
terms.whereItIs: Circulates in blood and lymph tissue; becomes active at stage 3 (antibody production).
terms.whyItMatters: B cells are the source of every antibody in the body — without them, the adaptive immune response couldn't happen at all.

terms.definition: A type of white blood cell that directly kills infected cells or helps coordinate the rest of the immune response.
terms.function: Some T cells destroy cells that are already infected with a pathogen; others act as coordinators, signaling B cells and other immune cells into action.
terms.whereItIs: Circulates in blood and lymph tissue, working alongside B cells throughout the response.
terms.whyItMatters: T cells add a second line of adaptive defense beyond antibodies — one that can find and remove cells a pathogen has already gotten inside of.

terms.definition: A long-lived B or T cell left behind after an infection that "remembers" a pathogen, enabling a much faster response if it returns.
terms.function: Stays in the body for years after the infection clears, ready to trigger rapid antibody production the instant it detects the same antigen again.
terms.whereItIs: Circulates quietly in blood and lymph tissue; shown resting at stage 5 of the diorama inside its faint standby halo.
terms.whyItMatters: Memory cells are the reason a second infection with the same germ is usually milder or doesn't happen at all — and the entire mechanism vaccines rely on.

terms.definition: The redness, heat, and swelling caused by increased blood flow and immune cells rushing to a site of infection or injury.
terms.function: Widens blood vessels and increases their permeability so white blood cells can reach the site of infection faster.
terms.whereItIs: Around any site of infection or injury, most familiar as the redness and puffiness around a cut.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflammation looks uncomfortable, but it's the immune system actively working, not just a side effect — it's part of what stage 2 (white blood cells respond) looks like from the outside.
